utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom. As I indicated yesterday, we'll have, at the end of the morning session, we'll have a break. But first, Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said we'll have a break, but of course I meant to say that we'll have a Status Conference at the end of the morning. Ms. Pilipovic, you may continue the last part of your cross-examination once the witness has been brought in. No other observations at this moment to make? Then please, Mr. Usher, would you bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mulaomerovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you as well. Ms. Pilipovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mulaomerovic.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We left off yesterday discussing the question of the conflict in Pofalici. Do you happen to know whether there were any casualties and fatalities in that conflict?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Our institution, the emergency service, worked at a higher intensity rate. There were more people wounded and injured that we had to take care of.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you say that patients were brought in to you from that particular area?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The wounded were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know or do you remember exactly how many?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't remember how many there were. But I do remember that there were quite a number of patients, or rather, wounded and injured persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that next to your building, the building of your institute, were the buildings of the Energoinvest company, the social insurance company, and you mentioned a few other buildings. Can you tell us whether, during the duration of the conflict, from 1992, that is to say September, up until 1994, August of 1994, whether those institutions were in fact working?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they were working. I think that those organisations had already stopped working. Some of them had been shelled, others had been set fire to, and I don't think they were operational during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in those -- there were any soldiers in those buildings and institutions?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I don't know that there were any soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that from September 1992 to August 1994 your building had been shot and hit on several occasions. Could you tell us, perhaps, when you say "several times," how many times that would be?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say tens of times. Perhaps there were 50 artillery projectiles and hundreds of other shots from firearms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was your building damaged?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, it was. The building had a flat roof, and we were able to count 17 hits on that flat roof of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you make a note of that? Did you record it, and did anybody come to the spot to ascertain the damage done? Was that recorded anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody came officially to ascertain the damage. We did so ourselves. And in the requests we made to the founders, we said that the roof had to be repaired, because it was quite obvious that damage had been done; they were easily visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As the director of your institution, was your signature registered in the court?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of that registered signature of yours, what authorisations and competences did you have?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was authorised to manage the institution and to sign all the documents; financial and others, orders and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The document that you were shown yesterday, which you looked at, and you were able to tell us that it was indeed the stamp of your institution, did you sign those documents and were you asked to sign them, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was asked to sign them, and I don't remember having signed them either. And I think I said that our protocol books are accessible to everybody authorised to look at them. They are public records, public documents, and they don't come under any sort of confidentiality. They are documents in our archives and can be used both by people authorised to do so and professionals, of course, as well, and anybody interested in specialising and using those facts and figures for their thesis.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me who in your institution authorises the use of these documents and access to them?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody, actually, has to give permission. This is stated in our rules and regulations. It states that our founders are the assembly of the canton and that medical assistance is of a public character and everything pertaining to that is public and that we are duty-bound to respect that and to inform the public and to be at the service of the public, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that concludes the

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: D24 into evidence as a Defence Exhibit, in view of the fact that the witness has identified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution whether there's any --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Realtime transcript read in error: "Mr. Blaxill"] The objection of the Prosecution is that the document has not been demonstrated to be relevant in issues in this case. It is a document which he has identified a stamp on, but beyond that, he cannot say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This Chamber will decide on this objection after the first break. I'd rather not spend too much time at this moment. I mean, the cross-examination has been concluded and I think we can decide on that, whether it's admitted into evidence, yes or no. Are there any other questions, perhaps, before I give the opportunity to the Prosecution to re-examine the witness by my colleagues? No questions. Then if there's any need for re-examination, please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said just now in your evidence, Doctor, that you counted 17 hits on the flat roof of the hospital. What did you mean when you said "hits"?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that the destruction done to the building was visible to the naked eye, that you could see it quite easily and count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What would you say caused those hits?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were caused by artillery weapons, which targeted and hit the roof of the building directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour, just have one moment, if you would indulge me, to confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the interval, to clarify matters, line 9:11:34 of the transcript, I did not hear Mr. Blaxill speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It must be a mistake. It was Mr. Stamp who was objecting against the admittance of the evidence of document D24. I think this will be corrected in the transcript. Please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. That concludes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mulaomerovic, this Chamber thanks you very much for coming -- I see that one of my colleagues still has a question, so if you please, still wait for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Do you have document D24 at hand?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please hand out D24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: As I was saying, we don't have a translation of the document. Would you please read numbers 1, 2, 3, and 15.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Point 1. The title is "Dead males." And under 1, Poduvnjak Anis, member of the OS, which means armed forces, the 1st of October, 1992. And then it continues to say: "1700 hours, armed conflict, one wound isolated injury, shell -- bullet head." So there's no full diagnosis there. Number 2 is Rizvanovic Huso, a civilian. The date is the 2nd of October, no date, at 1920 hours, "armed conflict, multiple injuries, a combined injury, shrapnel, left hand," and then the diagnosis follows: Vulnus explosivum brahi cum amputatio -- it says "vraci" [phoen], but it should be "brahi" -- vulnus explosivum thoracis, which means an explosive wound to the upper arm, including amputation of the arm, and an explosive injury to the chest. Number 3 is Palo Hajrudin. The date is the 5th of October, it says 1952. At 1130 hours, armed conflict, one RA. That's not a complete word. Isolated injury. Shrapnel, neck. And the diagnosis: vulnus explosivum regio coli, which means an explosive wound to the neck. 15 is Bojadzija Senad. It says a member of the OS, armed forces. The 13th of October, 1969 was his date of birth. At 10 hours, armed conflict, multiple injuries with a blunt object, multiple injuries, mortus adlatus detonatio, detonation or explosion, which means that the outcome was lethal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an excerpt from the protocol book. It doesn't actually tell me anything. It just confirms the particulars recorded in the protocol by somebody, by the person on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No other questions from the Bench. Then I again will start thanking you, Mr. Mulaomerovic, to have come such a far way and to inform this Court about what you know and what your experiences were. Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, would you please guide the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too. Thank you too, Your Honours, and thank you one and all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, do I understand well that the next witness that will be called by the Prosecution is Mr. Hajir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is indeed, Your Honour, and he will be taken by my learned friend Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The next witness is in fact Mr. Hajir, who will be taken by my learned friend, Mr. Michael Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand well that the time estimate for Dr. Hajir is two hours. Is that correct, Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I have no microphone here, but that is so, that is the maximum time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please come to a place where we can hear you, Mr. Blaxill. And I think the usher is -- yes, is bringing in Mr. Hajir. We'll wait until he arrives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, to answer Your Honour clearly, indeed the maximum time estimate for this witness was two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hajir, can you hear me in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Rule 90 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal requires you to make a solemn declaration of which the text will be handed out to you by the usher at this moment. Would you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hajir, please be seated. Welcome in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by Mr. Blaxill, who is a member of the Prosecution team. The Prosecution has called you as a witness in this case. Please proceed, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm grateful to you, Mr. President. Your Honours, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hajir. You've heard my name is Michael Blaxill and I will be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution in this case. Would you please commence by giving the Court your full name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Youssef Hajir, the 24th of June, 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And Dr. Hajir, I understand you are a surgeon by profession; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you were working as a surgeon in the traumatology clinic in Kosevo Hospital, Sarajevo, around the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what part of Sarajevo were you living in at that time?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: At that time, I was living at Vrace, which is part of the town, a district which is rather hilly. It is actually the start of Mount Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you at any time move from that location to another part of town to live?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No. From 1986 onwards I lived in that part of town until the war broke out, until the conflict, when I was forced -- that is to say, nobody forced me, but I saw that it was war, that the tanks were all around my house and that they were shooting at the city. So with my family and children, I had to find somewhere else to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And where did you go, sir?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: A friend of mine lived in Dobrinja, and he called me to come to him, because it was peaceful at that time in Dobrinja. And that's what I did; I went to him with my family and children to Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was it in April 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it also correct that Dobrinja is a former Olympic village that lies to the western end of Sarajevo, close to the airport? Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what sort of area was Dobrinja at the time you moved there? Was it a residential area, a commercial area, or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Dobrinja was built for the purposes of the 14th Olympiad, held in Sarajevo in 1984, and the building of Dobrinja started sometime in the 1970s and was completed by 1990. It is divided into several blocks, if I can call them that, apartment blocks, Dobrinja 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, C4, and the airport settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And are you saying by that that it is a predominantly residential area, or was?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: That's right. There were no factories or facilities of that kind. It was just a residential area. There were shops, there were three primary schools, there were two nurseries, there was a general medical clinic, there was a dentistry department, the infrastructure of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you have referred to the apartment complexes. Were these high-rise apartments, tall buildings with many occupants?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Not really. I don't think that the rules allowed building houses of more than six floors there because of the airport. There were some buildings, perhaps, which had seven or eight storeys, but generally they were six-storey buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And shortly after you moved to Dobrinja to get away from armed conflict elsewhere in Sarajevo, did the situation in Dobrinja change?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sorry. Shortly after you moved to Dobrinja, did the situation change in terms of the existence of any armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: When I came to Dobrinja, I had to take the main road towards town, and then some people were running because there was shooting, and they were afraid. I don't think there were any casualties, but it was dangerous to pass by that way because there was some shooting all the time. However, in the settlement itself, when I arrived, there was no major shelling or sniper activity of any kind until the beginning of May perhaps, May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And from what you say, Doctor, did shelling of Dobrinja commence after that date, and likewise, sniping?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: From that date on, yes, from the beginning of May until the end of the war, it never ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, were any civilian buildings and civilian areas hit by shells?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, you see: There were no military units there at the beginning. It wasn't an organised army. How could you organise an army when the JNA was the sole army in Bosnia that was recognised? At the beginning, the people who tried to do something, if I can put it that way, were organised groups of young men, say 10 or 15 youngsters who would go round in cars with light weapons. They would go round the settlement. They might have had a pistol or a rifle, but no major arsenal of weapons of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure, Mr. President, but I thought I heard the word "Muslims" quoted. The English transcript said "people." I thought I heard the word "Muslims." Could the witness please be asked to repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please invite the witness to repeat, and perhaps specifically ask him whether he used the word "Muslims," which does not appear in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, you've heard Mr. President's request. Could you repeat what you've just said about the people going round defending, and could you confirm whether or not you have used the word "Muslim" in that context.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No, I didn't use that word at all. I don't remember saying "Muslims" at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it has not been said, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I would like you first to verify, perhaps with your colleague, before making these time-taking interventions just based on a -- as far as I can see now, a wrong hearing of what has been said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And Dr. Hajir, from what you said, moving on, can you tell us, then, where were the shells landing when they were shelling Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: All over the place. When I was thinking of where I could find shelter for my children, I simply couldn't find a place that would be safe and protect them from injury. So really, it was all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And likewise with the -- you've referred to sniping. Was that sniping on just specific locations or was -- or were there danger points all over Dobrinja as a result of sniping?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: These are apartment buildings built of concrete and steel, and if you know the direction from which the fire was coming - and at first we knew it was coming from Mojmilo, from Lukavica, from Dobrinja 4 - then you could seek shelter behind a building to avoid being hit by a sniper. That was the only way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And where you have stated the fire coming from, can you tell us, please, who was controlling those areas, like at that time, Mojmilo, Lukavica, Dobrinja 4?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, you see, Dobrinja is such a geographic location that it was simply surrounded on all four sides. The Lukavica barracks was one of the largest in the former Yugoslavia. Then there were the airports, the airstrips, until the UN or SFOR took over. Then the village of Nedzarici. And from the fourth side, that is, where the road leads into the centre of town, there is the Mojmilo hill, where again certain tanks and APCs were positioned, so that communication with the city centre was cut off entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And who were the forces who effected that isolation of Dobrinja? Who were the actual army that were doing it?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: The JNA and paramilitary formations which had already appeared in Sarajevo in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would those forces be ones that commonly became identified as the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it correct that in fact there was a change in position by June of that year and Dobrinja did re-establish some direct contact with the city of Sarajevo? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Have you noticed civilian casualties being sustained in Dobrinja during the months from May that caused you to take any action yourself as regards medical facilities?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I had already mentioned, sir, that there was no organised Bosnian army at the time. The people that did come out, so to speak, did so to protect their families. We, or rather, not myself because I was a guest there, but people in Dobrinja organised guard duty, so one of the tenants would be on duty at the main entrance so that nobody could come in to kill people or frighten people among the paramilitaries. Most of these, I can't give you a percentage, but the vast majority were civilians, they were not soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you notice that there were civilian casualties being sustained, and did that prompt you to take any action to set up a medical facility?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, you see, as this isolation of Dobrinja was really complete, it was very dangerous to ask people to carry an injured person over the Mojmilo hill. There was a road that people could use over the hill to the village of Surakino Selo and enter town from there, but it was very dangerous to send four healthy men to carry an injured man, and you never knew whether he would recover or not, to save him. So that, as I am a surgeon and I specialise in traumas, walking around Dobrinja on a daily basis, I saw that during the daytime there weren't any major activities, but the shelling was mostly at night, at least at the beginning. Later on, this changed a bit. So together with many other people who were medical men, doctors, technicians, nurses. We felt helpless because we didn't have any material that we needed for surgery. You need a lot of equipment. You need sterilisation and ... So we agreed that if we could find some surgical material, we would provide aid to those people. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you: Did you in fact set up an emergency room or something equivalent to a hospital facility in Dobrinja; and if so, when was that operational?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: At the beginning of May, these friends of mine called me and said that dozens of people had been injured in putting out a fire in a school. I can't remember the name of that school just now. Anyway, in trying to extinguish the fire, as it had been shelled, they called me out to see whether there was anything we could do to assist them. So we opened a dental clinic. We found some material and some also medical material in the local clinic, and I managed to operate on those people. I started in the afternoon and went on working until 4.00 a.m. Four or five of them could not be sent home. They had serious injuries that could lead to subsequent haemorrhage and complications so I asked the neighbours to provide some mattresses and things, and I kept the patients there, and I stayed with them, of course, together with a nurse, two technicians, and another doctor, a general practitioner. And we stayed there with them. And from that day on, there were injured people coming in on a daily basis and the needs were increasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I may move forward in time, Dr. Hajir, as time is pressing on us. For the period from September of 1992 through to August of 1994 is the period on which I would like to concentrate. And could you tell us, firstly, did the shelling and the sniping of civilians continue from September 1992 onwards through 1993 and into 1994?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Throughout -- you see, every day there were periods of ceasefires, but you still had to be careful, because there would be isolated shells. But those days were few and far between, days with reduced shelling and reduced sniping. On an average, we had 10 to 15 injuries a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you say that is an average. Do you mean by that, Doctor -- do you mean that that was an average through the whole period? In other words, if we take the whole of 1993, would that have been still the daily average, roughly?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I gave you an average for the whole war, but 1993 it could have been a higher number, but I have no statistics, so I can't be precise about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And of the casualties that you received into your hospital in Dobrinja, can you tell us how many were civilian patients and how many may have been military patients, i.e., wounded soldiers?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: In 1992, there were really very few soldiers, maybe up to 3 per cent of all injuries, because there was no army. The army was in the process of being formed. I think it was in August or September, something like that, I don't know exactly. So for you to be able to say that any of the injured were soldiers, during the war, I don't know what to say. The vast majority of the injured throughout the war were civilians, because the military had a certain system of shifts. They would go to the front every five days or something. And there were few occasions when they were in actual direct confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sir, would the persons treated for wounds in your Dobrinja hospital have included women or children or elderly people?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. A shell makes no selection. If you fire a shell in a housing area, it's only logical to expect that among the casualties there would be women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what about such casualties, women and children, in respect of the issue of sniping? Did you treat women and/or children or the elderly in respect of bullet wounds from the sniping that occurred?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: During the war, there were various news agencies, reporters, CNN, and others, and they asked me what was the most difficult moment for me in the wartime, during the war. For me, the worst was when a 7-year-old child was hit directly in the heart. This sniper must have been able to see that it was a child. He has special sights. And he was hit directly in the heart. And during the five minutes it took to bring the child into hospital, he had died. So that was not an isolated case; there were many. There were mutilations and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, as regards the civilian population of Dobrinja at that time through from September 1992 to the middle of 1994, what did the people have to do to obtain water and food? Was it readily available? Did they have to go to places to get it?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: That was indeed the worst side of the war. To cut off the water, 300.000 or 350.000 inhabitants of Dobrinja at the time. I don't know how to explain it to you. None of us counts how many litres of water we consume per day, but you can imagine when one has to carry a five-litre jerrycan and queue up at a well to get it, and it would happen not once, several times, that, among the crowd lining up for water, a shell would fall. I apologise for speaking like this; it took me three years after the war for my brain to recover to be able to think and work properly because all those injuries passed through my hands. I was in charge of the hospital and the logistics of the hospital, and so on. So it's very hard for me to remember numbers and things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you, when -- you have said numbers are difficult to remember, but can you give us an indication of the total number of persons that you treated in your hospital in Dobrinja during the war? Just a rough figure.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: There were several thousand injuries. I didn't count them. But somebody told me about 16.000, among whom there were many who were injured passing through the tunnel. This tunnel was about 120, 130 centimetres in height, so you had to bend down to pass through, and every other person who passed through had to straighten himself up - the tunnel was about 800 metres long - and he would hurt himself on the iron bars in the tunnels, so there were injuries of that kind too. There were other injuries, not solely those due to the fire. There was also self-inflicted injuries, but these were small in number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you give us any idea, then, of the total number of casualties from shelling and sniping who passed through your Dobrinja hospital? Clearly, if you can't remember, that's -- please say so.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I cannot, really. Please, it really is difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall whether your hospital itself was ever hit by any shell fire or by any sniping?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes, several times. There were hits around the hospital, because the hospital was on the ground floor, and above it there were seven or eight storeys, I don't know exactly, so it couldn't be hit but the building itself was hit several times. There were shells in front of the hospital, next to the hospital. There were medical staff injured who would be coming and going from work. So I'm really very bad with figures, but you can check this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, was your -- was the building in which you had the hospital marked in any way to indicate that it was a medical facility?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: At first, I must admit, it wasn't. It never occurred to us, because it was an improvised hospital. I told you, it was just a group of medical workers who organised themselves, and I must be quite honest, it didn't occur to me at the time. But two or three months later, somebody drew our attention to this. So we didn't put a sign right on top of the building, but just above the actual hospital floor, a Red Cross sign, two or three months into the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've referred to the shelling in respect of the hospital. What about sniping? Were any people sniped at in or near the hospital?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I don't know. It was our good fortune that the hospital was well protected, so the hospital itself was not sniped at, because it was difficult to reach it with a sniper. Probably that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Dr. Hajir, did you have any ambulances to collect casualties and bring them to your hospital?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes, there were several ambulances. We used the iron from the sewerage systems, lids, the lids, the covers, and we protected the vehicles with them to protect the people inside from sniping and shells that may not hit the vehicle itself directly. At first, we used various heavy books and lined the walls of the van with these books so that the sniper bullet couldn't pass through and hit somebody inside. And all these ambulances were marked as ambulances. I think one that was used for the longest period of time I suggested should be put in a museum to show how many holes it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall how many holes were in it?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No. No. A large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, in what manner were your ambulances marked to point them out to be ambulances?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: With the Red Cross sign that an ambulance usually has. We didn't have the lights, but we just had this Red Cross sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've referred to one ambulance being shot at and hit. What about other ambulances? Was this the same fate for all your vehicles?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes, the same. It was extremely dangerous to drive them, you know. Our vehicles would drive at 120 kilometres an hour to reach Kosevo or the cantonal hospital. If we were overcrowded with patients, then we had to transport some patients to those hospitals. If it was a neurosurgical injury, an injury of the thorax or another complicated injury of large blood vessels, then these people had to be transported to other hospitals, and it was very dangerous to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And in fact, that was the next question I would ask you, Doctor. In connection with transporting people on for further treatment in other hospitals, did you find that you had to take any special precautions, or could you do that task safely?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Drivers were very brave, so no one tried to evade their duties. They always carried out their duties and came back. Two drivers were injured, one was killed. I always listened to their advice, and whatever we could do to follow it, we would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Hajir, I would ask you: Later on in the war, when clearly defences were better, let us say later in 1993 and into 1994, were there any military installations or military presence close to your hospital? By that, I mean the ABiH defence.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There was a brigade, the Dobrinja Brigade, which was formed later, but most of these people had light arms. So I really never did my military service, I have no understanding of weapons. But people were coming from town to assist as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That being said, were any military stationed actually in your hospital in the latter stages, or in the apartments above, or was that still civilian?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: In hospital, I can say under oath, and there were never people stationed there. Soldiers would come occasionally, but it was never a military facility. In fact, I warned the commander that they mustn't even shoot within a diameter of 50 metres of the hospital because the lives of all those people would be at risk. So that there were none in the hospital. Whether there were any in the apartments, I really don't know. But a military facility, a barracks or something used by the military for military purposes, that did not exist. These were small apartments, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'll turn your memory, if I may, Doctor, to one incident. Do you remember any particular incident occurring on Bajram in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: My learned friend has a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just so that we are quite sure, I don't know whether the witness mentioned in his last statement which hospital he was referring to so that we know exactly what we're talking about. Because a moment ago he spoke about Kosevo and other hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although this would be a perfect question for cross-examination, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, so that you will not interrupt the examination-in-chief. But, Mr. Blaxill, if you would be in a position to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I certainly will.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, you've just been referring to "the hospital" in response to my questions about military presence. Were you referring, of course, to your hospital in Dobrinja? Is that right? Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Hajir, I refer again to the matter of Bajram, 1993. Do you recall a particular incident that day in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I know that on that day, in the morning - I believe that's how it was - all of a sudden we heard that there was a large number of injured. Some football match was being played, there was some sort of competition in Dobrinja 3. I think it was Dobrinja 3, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure, I really don't know whether it was. I think it was B, Dobrinja 3B . Two or three shells - I'm not quite sure - fell. It was a quiet morning. All of a sudden you could hear two or three shells. I'm really not sure about this. But all of a sudden these shells -- there was a large number of injured. We've never had so many injured arriving in the hospital at one time. The entire hospital, all the wards in the hospital, were full. Unfortunately, there are various cases in history and various writers provide various statistics on the number of those who were injured, but what I do know for sure is that those who came to the hospital did not all come at that time, because there was an enormous number of seriously wounded people. Some people perhaps came into the hospital in the evening or the following day or two days later. But as I say, there are various statistics, but it was about 130 to 140 injured. And in our morgue - I'm not sure of the exact number, I don't want to raise controversial issues, but I think there were about 130 or -- 113 to 14 dead. Don't take this for something that's a hundred per cent sure, but I think those are the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, I will ask you a little bit more about record-making in the future, so I would like, in a sense, a yes or no answer. Would any record have been kept by your hospital of the treatment of those patients?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: They attempted to keep records, there was a service that kept records, but I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, there's just one small question I would ask you: When shells landed on Dobrinja, were you ever able to hear anything of the shell prior to the explosion? Did it make any sound as it came in?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I might just take a moment, Your Honours, to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged for your indulgence, Your Honours. We will not keep you very much longer, so my time estimate, I think, was over-generous to the time we required. I will just move on to the last topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, I've mentioned the question of records. Can you give us an indication of how your records were kept in the hospital, or the difficulties you had so doing?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: The Dobrinja hospital was an improvised one. It didn't have such services. It didn't have these various services which kept records. So we had to do everything from scratch. There were people who were responsible for keeping certain records, as far as this was possible. But when everything is totally chaotic and when you have 130, 140 people who are injured and who arrive and when you just can't pass through those injured people, then it's very difficult to keep records in such a situation in an adequate way. You can always object to this. I was not -- I was personally not a hundred per cent content with this - I'm a precise person - but I wasn't happy with the way the records were being kept. These perhaps are details, but I'm a perfectionist, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, even with the limitations that you faced, I presume that you were able, at some point, to have records created in respect of a number of patients. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look in a moment, Dr. Hajir, at some documents that we will show to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are the two listed exhibits I would like to have shown to Dr. Hajir, and they are numbered 1183 and 2506A. I will make one point in respect of these at this point, Your Honours, and that is this: ERN number ranges are given because these documents are selected from batches of documents. They are relevant to certain victims; other documents in the batch were not relevant to the victims. And as a result, the specific ERNs will not be consequential from start to finish of the range, because this is simply a selection of documents, if that assists you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that is an explanation that will help us. Yes, would you please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, I'd ask you, sir, just to look through the documents that have been placed in front of you, and the question is very simple in that: Are you able to recognise those documents, and do they represent records from your Dobrinja hospital in respect of the persons named in them?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: These are documents from the hospital. I don't remember the individual persons. You know, I can't remember the names of these persons, but these documents are from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it correct, Dr. Hajir, that your signature appears indeed as the senior consultant on a number of those documents?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Hajir.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I, in fact, have just one last question, if -- I'll wait until Your Honours have finished looking at the documents, as you see fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed with ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have just one last question, Dr. Hajir. Can you just tell the Chamber the very first time you performed a surgical operation in Dobrinja, what were the conditions you were working under, the very first surgical procedure there, sir?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Impossible conditions. It was really necessary to have a lot of courage, but there's nothing to be done about it. The people had to be helped. It was on a simple examination table. One was on one's knees, using -- we were using stomatological instruments. We had very few instruments, but the important thing was to stop the bleeding and to prevent the people from dying because of loss of blood or because of totally banal things. But it was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What about the light? What did you use for light?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: We used simple candles, three candles. They would carry three candles and approach the wounded with these candles. It was very dangerous. The situation was one that you would find in a cave, but there was nothing else to be done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I regret my ignorance as to the technical word for those instruments, but does that mean they were dental tools that you were using to perform surgery?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes. They were instruments, sort of pliers, if I can call them in this way. Various instruments that dentists use for their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, that concludes the questions that I have for you, sir. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I thank Your Honours. That concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Blaxill. We've still got enough time to start with the cross-examination, so if Ms. Pilipovic would proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Hello. In the course of the main cross-examination [as interpreted] you said that when the conflict started, you were in Vrace. When the conflict started, you left Vrace with your family. When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: About the 18th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you lived at Vrace, what conflict existed there, and between which sides?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, there were rumours going round that it was a war, things like that, and most people were psychologically prepared for that, for something like that. I know what I saw. Below my house, there were two tanks, for instance, and behind the bypass at Vrace -- I don't know how far you know the city of Sarajevo, but as you go to Vrace, there was a tank on one side and another tank on the other side, and around the police academy or school there was a machine-gun or something like that. I don't know what it was but there was a weapon positioned there. That's what I was able to see. I didn't go anywhere else. I just went to the hospital several times and back, up until the 18th of April. There were checkpoints. They would look at my papers. But people knew me and respected me and I could pass with my ID card. After the 18th, that was more difficult. It was very difficult to move around. There was shooting --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. In your answer, you mentioned the police school. Do you happen to know that there was a conflict in the police school; and if you do know about that, could you tell us between whom the conflict was.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I did hear there was a clash of some kind between the police, the policemen who were there, and some others. I can't give you an exact answer. I really don't know exactly what happened, but I do know that there was a clash.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the ethnic composition of the police force in Sarajevo was?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were Serbs and Croats in the police force?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the clash in the police school broke out between the ethnic Serbs and ethnic Muslims in the police force, the policemen?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No, I really didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you came to Dobrinja. What part of Dobrinja did you come to?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Dobrinja 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that Dobrinja was divided into five parts. Could you explain what those five parts were. What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, as it was being built, it was given names, and there was Dobrinja 1, 2, the Cemadjesta [phoen] area, and then as they went on constructing the buildings, there was 3, 4, and 5. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Dobrinja, you said you moved around, but did you go to all the parts of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't do that, you see, because the main road with the shopping area was where people would walk around, talk about the war, exchange stories of what they had heard on the news. But no, I wasn't able to move around the whole of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Dobrinja 5?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Dobrinja 5, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I had no business there. My job didn't take me there, so I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: However, madam, if I may just add one thing. If you're talking about the whole -- throughout the war, there was a clinic belonging to the hospital there, so I went to see that outpatient's department once or twice, whether they had everything they needed. So that's the only occasion that I went to Dobrinja 5, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While you moved around Dobrinja, did you happen to notice organised groups of young men with light weapons, as you said today, a moment ago? And it's in the transcript. You said that at 9:30.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes. On two or three occasions I did come across these young men with some rifles. I would see two or three cars moving around in circles in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who those young men were?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No. At least, not at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about later on? Did you learn who they were?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Later on, I learnt that they were the defenders, people who were there to defend themselves from the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to meet any of them?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, they would come by, bringing in wounded and injured persons. They came to the hospital so I did come into contact with some of them, yes, although I didn't know them previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When they came to you, did they have the light weapons that you say they had in their possession?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Sometimes they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where they were put up?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the Dobrinja residential area? What are the districts bordering on Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: There is Mojmilo, which is the Olympic village and which was built in 1984 to accommodate the journalists, and later on people took up residence in these apartments; then there's Lukavica. You know the place called Lukavica and the Lukavica barracks, whether that is to the east or wherever. Then there is the airport and the airport settlement, the old airport and the new airport. There's an airport and then a road and then behind that there's Butmir and Ilijas and so on. And on that same side, towards town, facing town, you have Nedzarici, the barracks, and the settlement, or rather, Nedzarici was the name of the village originally.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about Vojnicko Polje and Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes, that's across, opposite Mojmilo but Alipasino Polje is further down, towards town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the Vojnicko Polje and Alipasino Polje apartment blocks? What were they built of?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but I think they were built of concrete.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How high were these buildings?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, they're fairly high. They're high-rise buildings. Some of them are higher, others are lower, but how many storeys they have, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about the Nedzarici settlement?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Nedzarici were mostly low buildings, one or two storeys at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that when you arrived in Dobrinja, that at Mojmilo, the Yugoslav army had set up positions.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: On the hill, Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Mojmilo hill. That's what I meant. Do you happen to know whether throughout the conflict, as you say, from April 1992 until the end of the conflict, for us, 1994 is relevant, whether the Yugoslav army units were on that hill at that time?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When were they there?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: They were there at the beginning; in April, May, and June. In June, the military police, if I can call it that - and it was actually called the military police, led by Kerim Lucarevic - they hit that part. So I don't know. And that position was destroyed, as far as I was able to see and as far as I know. I think that happened in June, which means that it was there for two, possibly three months.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Kerim Lucarevic and the military police. What was he in the military police?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: He was the commander, the chief of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That military police, what was -- within what formation was it established, if you know?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know how many members the military police numbered?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: May we agree that you said that the military police, whose commander was Kerim Lucarevic, in June took control of Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, no, it didn't take control of the point, no. It just -- that is to say, the tanks and the APCs, they were destroyed, but they didn't actually go up to Mojmilo. They didn't mount Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers, after Kerim Lucarevic police climbed up Mojmilo hill, were there any soldiers during the war there?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I don't know whether you believe me or not, but I really don't know. It's a hill, and Lukavica lies the other side of it. So it was dangerous. It was an open space. You can see it from Gavrica hill. You can see it very well. And that's where the tanks were stationed. And they were strong tank formations up there. So I myself really didn't see them, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know where the headquarters of Kerim Lucarevic's command of the military police was? Where was his staff and headquarters?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't remember now. Perhaps it will come to me. If you ask me later on, I might remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that the brigade was set up on Dobrinja after the BH army was formed. Since when was that brigade up at Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: The commander of the brigade was there when I came to Dobrinja. He was sitting about in the local community and talking. Now, whether he was assigned there by anybody, I can't say. I don't really know. But I do know that he was there, he was talking to the people, he wanted to organise the people, and that kind of thing. Later on, by decision of the Presidency - I don't know when that decision came, whether in August or whenever - to declare a state of war, then the army was set out and then that brigade was established later on, and he remained the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You came to Dobrinja on the 18th of April, 1992, did you not?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you talk to the commander of the brigade for the first time?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: He was not the brigade commander; he was just a man who was interested in that -- there wasn't a brigade. The brigade wasn't formed yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But you said there was a brigade and that he was the commander. Now I'm asking you now when the brigade was formed.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: That was later on, not at the beginning. I said that at the beginning there were no soldiers. There was no army. I went chronologically. Following a decision by the Presidency to declare a state of war, then the army began to be formed, the BH army, and that's when the brigade was officially established in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you when that was.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I don't know. Towards the end of 1992. I can't say exactly, give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what that gentleman's name was, the man who later became commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Ismet Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, did you know then, or did you happen to learn whether he was an army man?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No. He was an employee in the Energoinvest company.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how he came to command the brigade?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I can't explain that. I have already said that he was somebody who was interested in things like that. He tried to organise a defence. Now, I really can't say. I can't tell you. I'm here under oath, so I would say, had I known that he was cooperating with someone, but I don't know, neither did I learn about that later on. All I do know is that he was interested in setting up a defence and he started organising these groups, probably, and later on, as he had organised the groups, he was -- he became the commander. He was appointed commander. That's what I think. I can't say for sure, but those are my impressions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you came to Dobrinja on the 18th of April because it was peaceful in Dobrinja. Can you explain why Mr. Ismet Hadzic walked around Dobrinja, trying to organise, as you said, these people?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, even a blind man living in that part of town, that part of Sarajevo and Bosnia, would know that a war was imminent. Towns were falling one by one, Zvornik and so on. Delegations would go, as far as I recall from television, Biljana Plavsic went to Bijeljina when the paramilitary formations entered. So even a blind man would clearly see that war was imminent and that war was coming. You didn't have to have much intelligence to realise that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you a member of a party?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No, never. Well, let me be quite clear. I was a member of Haris's party. I was there for perhaps a year. But after that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Immediately after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said today that there was a barracks in Nedzarici and in Lukavica. Do you happen to know how many barracks existed in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I don't know. I could enumerate the barracks. There was one at Bistrik. There was another one up there - what's the name of the place - Jajce or whatever, the building above Sarajevo. Those were Tito's barracks. Those were the barracks that I know. I don't know any others.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When the brigade was formed in Dobrinja, where was the brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: The headquarters were in a ground floor building, 150 metres away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was this ground floor facility in a residential block or in a commercial building?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, it was a commercial building, but there were also some apartments in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know how many soldiers the brigade numbered?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Asked by my learned friend, you said that you remembered an incident that took place on Bajram. Would you tell us when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Madam, I told you straight away, and I hope you'll understand me and the efforts I'm making and my general fatigue, because every injured person went through my hands, but I think that it was sometime in June 1993 or thereabouts. I really can't give you an exact date, because injured people and wounded people kept coming in. There was a constant flow. And when you're doing your job, when you're out to save the lives of people, it's difficult to remember things like dates. But I would say thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you form the health institution at Dobrinja which later on became a hospital?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I answered that question a moment ago. It was at the beginning of June, perhaps the 5th, 7th, 8th, I'm not quite sure, but it was the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And which part of Dobrinja was that in?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Dobrinja 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your hospital, did you treat people from Dobrinja 1, 3, 5 as well, and 4?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Not only them, but everybody that came to us. Dobrinja is in a geographical position that it forms an exit to Sarajevo through the tunnel, so it was an entrance/exit point, with many people passing by. There was shelling at the entrance and exit on many occasions, and people, within they weren't using the tunnel, they had to run across the airstrip to come to Butmir, and many people were injured crossing. So people coming from town into Dobrinja and going from Dobrinja into town. There were a lot of people and a lot of injured and wounded people as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the brigade's headquarters were located on the ground floor of a building that was an apartment block and an office building. Do you happen to know the position of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I really don't know. As I say, I'm not a soldier. I never carried a rifle, and I wasn't really interested in anything like that, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In June, when the incident occurred, according to you, you said that it was Dobrinja 3B.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Well, that's what I think. That's what people said, that it was Dobrinja 3B.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take in those patients?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes. All the patients came to me, and I have already told you that we had the largest number of patients ever that day, so you couldn't go into any of the rooms. You had to step between the bodies on tiptoe. We transported a number to town, and then 90 of them were in fact treated in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: May I intervene for one moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Looking at the transcript, it's really a matter of clarification. My learned friend was questioning about the starting of the hospital and the month of June was referred to. We then get to an incident and a month of June is referred to, but we haven't clarified the years, and I think we're talking different years. I think it would assist to have that matter clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please clarify this, Ms. Pilipovic, and at the same time, think of a suitable moment for our break. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, sir. The hospital was set up in June of what year?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Not June; May. May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You're going to mix me up. You said June. Tell us which year.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: It was the 5th of May sometime -- the 5th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what year did the incident take place that was mentioned? And we were talking about the football match.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: In 1993, I suppose. I really don't know dates, but I do know when the hospital was established, whereas the stadium incident was 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think this is a good moment to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. We'll then adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we bring in the witness, I still owe you a decision on the objection raised by the Prosecution against the admittance into evidence -- admission into evidence of document prenumbered D24, which has been shown to the witness Dr. Mulaomerovic. The Chamber agrees with the Prosecution that no attention whatsoever has been paid to the content of this document, so the mere fact on whether there was a stamp on it, whether there was any signature on it, shows no relevance, as long as you do not go into the content of the document as such. So to that extent, the objection should be sustained. On the other hand, the Chamber is entitled to ask the parties, to request the parties to introduce any additional evidence, and as a matter of fact, the Chamber implicitly has done so by putting questions regarding the content of this document after the objection was raised. So therefore, although the objection as such was justified at that moment, nevertheless, the document will be admitted into evidence but based upon the questioning regarding the content by the Chamber itself. I think then we can proceed with the cross-examination. Would you please bring in Mr. Hajir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst he's being brought in, might I ask when you propose to have the Status Conference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I propose to have the Status Conference from 1.00 until a quarter to 2.00. So we'll have a break which is a bit longer than usual, since the courtroom has to be prepared for the Status Conference. I therefore suggest that we have another break from half past 12.00 until 1.00, half an hour, and then have a Status Conference for three quarters of an hour. Ms. Pilipovic, you may proceed. And I point out to you that we are approximately at 50 per cent of the time used by the Prosecution in their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, we were speaking about the incident that occurred in June 1993. Did you admit the patients who were injured at that match?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your institution, did you keep a record of the admission of patients?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: There's a protocol that we improvised, a protocol into which we entered the names of those patients and the year of birth and what kind of injury they had. And when patients were admitted to stay, a case history had to be kept, how he was injured, how he was treated, what the operation was, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you enter into this protocol the fact whether it was a civilian or a military man that was injured?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Does your institution have any such document?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: It does not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I say "document," I mean a protocol. In your institution, do you have this protocol that you kept for the period from the time you founded the hospital for as long as it was operational? And I'm specifically interested in the period up to August 1994. Is there a protocol in your institution?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: All the documents of the hospital, when the hospital was closed, was handed over to the museum of the city of Sarajevo. Therefore, those protocols do exist and they are in the museum of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me, please: Would that be in the archives of the city of Sarajevo as part of the museum?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When, on the 1st of June, when the incident occurred, you were admitting patients who, as you said, were injured during that football match, did you list them, and in what way? What entries did you make when admitting a patient? What entries in that protocol?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago: The first and last name, the year of birth, and the kind of injury. If the patient is being transported into town, then we note "transfer" or "transport," and with a piece of paper saying what kind of injury, what was done, whether there was infusion, any kind of surgery done. This piece of paper accompanies the patient when he is transported to other hospitals in town. As for the other patients who remained with us, the minor injuries were treated, and a document, a piece of paper, a report, was drawn up saying what the diagnosis was, what was done, what medicines were prescribed, and the doctor signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In that document on admission, did you note down whether it was a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When admitting patients on the 1st of June, you said you admitted roughly 140, and there were 13 or 14 persons killed. Did you note down for these people whether they were soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR
utterances.text: To be quite honest, we never took note of whether a patient was a military man, a civilian, or anything else. We didn't take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to show the witness a document which the Defence was given by the Prosecution, X2506, and I will show the witness two documents, number 00267861 and 00267862, for the witness to confirm whether these are documents from the hospital at Dobrinja and to read out what these documents say - this is very brief, very short - to tell us whether this is a document from the hospital and whose signature it bears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will that be one document or two documents, so in order to prenumber them? Because I expect you to tender them into evidence and not just have them marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the moment, the Defence will not tender them until the witness authenticates them. They are the same document but only on two pages. The point is for the witness to tell us whether this is one and the same document coming from the institution that he worked in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic. Ms. Pilipovic, do you have copies for the Bench and the Prosecution is aware of what document it is, or do you provide copies at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friends have that document, because it was given to us by them. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if you have got 5.000 documents and it's not indicated before which document you'll use, I think it will be time-saving if you provide with a copy, or otherwise I give the Prosecution the time at this moment to find this document. And the Bench certainly has no copies yet, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may say at this point it appears not to be one of the ones selected that forms part of our exhibits that we propose to tender, so we would appreciate if we could have copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have any copies available, Ms. Pilipovic, because it would take too much time to find them among 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on these pages, we have the number of the document, and we can see the document on the screen. And I hope it will be sufficient for all of us to see it on the screen and for the witness to tell us whether it comes from this institution. But in the future, I will certainly make sure to copy these documents. But they come under X2506, and there are 100 documents in that batch. X2506. We see the document on the screen now. Could the witness tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will allow you one question whether the witness recognises this document which is on our screen now. But if you have any further questions related to the document or if you intend to tender that document into evidence, I'd like to have copies made, and perhaps they can be made even during trial so that you proceed and have copies within a couple of minutes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sorry to have to interrupt, and thank you for giving me the floor. We have formally asked this Tribunal, on several occasions, to give us a legal assistant in court, precisely to be able to deal with problems of this kind. We cannot have discussions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I will allow you to raise these kind of issues during the Status Conference.
